**Setup.** Sort the numbers: $a_1 \le a_2 \le \dots \le a_{10}$. The condition "any three sum to more than 7" is equivalent to $a_1+a_2+a_3 > 7$, since the smallest three-sum is the binding case. Because $a_3$ is the largest of $a_1, a_2, a_3$, we have $3a_3 \ge a_1+a_2+a_3 > 7$, so $a_3 > 7/3$. Every $a_k$ with $k \ge 3$ is at least $a_3$, so $a_k > 7/3$ for $k \ge 3$.

**a) No.** The largest possible sum of seven numbers is $a_4+\dots+a_{10}$. Each of these seven numbers exceeds $7/3$, so
$$a_4+\dots+a_{10} > 7\cdot\tfrac{7}{3} = \tfrac{49}{3} > 16.$$
Thus some seven-element sum exceeds 16, so the condition "every seven-sum is less than 16" fails.

**b) Yes.** Take all ten numbers equal to $t$. The conditions become:
- Three-sums: $3t > 7 \iff t > 7/3$.
- Five-sums: $5t < 12 \iff t < 12/5$.

Since $7/3 \approx 2.333 < 2.4 = 12/5$, the interval $(7/3,\,12/5)$ is nonempty. For example, $t = 2.35 = 47/20$ gives $3t = 7.05 > 7$ and $5t = 11.75 < 12$. Every three-sum and every five-sum then satisfies the required bounds.

**Answers:**
- a) No, because the sum of the seven largest numbers exceeds $49/3 > 16$.
- b) Yes, for example ten numbers all equal to $2.35$.

Final answer: a) No; b) Yes (e.g., all ten numbers equal to 2.35).
